newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU Commission tackles investment restrictions.
newsitem.headline: EU Commission tackles investment restrictions.

text.p: The European Commission is slowly increasing pressure on national capitals to abolish restrictions on the way investment and pension funds are managed and invested.
Pension and investment funds -- such as equity and money markey funds -- represent total assets of $1.3 trillion each in the European Union.

But their development is hampered by national restrictions, which say, for example, that assets must be invested mostly in local bonds or allow only a tiny proportion to be invested in foreign instruments.
This flies in the face of the European Union's single market rules which provide for the free movement of capital.

"We are currently considering, with the help of our legal service, possible infringement cases against certain member states," said Mario Monti, the European commissioner responsible for making the single market work.
Speaking at a meeting of the European Federation of Investment Funds and Companies (FEFSI), Monti did not name any countries. But Commission sources said Germany and Austria were the first targets.

Monti, referring to an ill-fated Commission attempt to revise EU legislation on the Undertakings for Collective Investment in Transferable Securities (UCITS) to include cash funds, money-market funds and master-feeder funds, said he was seeking "an early agreement" on a "slimmed down" version of the 1993 draft.
EU finance ministers asked the Commission early in 1995 to revise the draft following years of sterile negotiations. The Commission has the support of a small minority of countries led by Britain.
Another Commission proposal to create an EU-wide market for pension funds, which was first proposed in 1991, is also deadlocked.

The draft sought to limit to 60 percent the amount of pension fund assets that national governments may require to be invested in instruments denominated in their own currency -- the so-called currency matching rule -- but a majority could only agree on 80 percent.

EU states say the restrictions are needed on prudential grounds. But the Commission strongly contests this arguing that individuals would benefit from lower risks and higher returns if pension fund managers were able to invest in the most efficient way throughout the Union.

The Commission has also challenged national restrictions on pension funds. The procedure could ultimately be taken to the European Court of Justice if no progress is made. -- Brussels Newsroom 32 2 287 6800
